reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A premalignant epithelial tumour of the ampulla of Vater with recognised potential to progress through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but may present with obstructive jaundice, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or occult gastrointestinal bleeding
Strongly associated with familial adenomatous polyposis, in whom duodenal and ampullary surveillance is an established part of care
Best assessed at side-viewing duodenoscopy, which allows direct visualisation and biopsy of the papilla
Endoscopic ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging help stage the lesion and detect intraductal extension or invasion
Biopsies can underestimate the grade, so a focus of carcinoma may only be found after complete excision
Endoscopic ampullectomy is appropriate for benign lesions confined to the papilla, while invasion or extensive intraductal spread favours surgical resection
reference.pathophysiology: Ampullary adenomas arise from the glandular epithelium at the confluence of the common bile and pancreatic ducts with the duodenum. Accumulation of genetic alterations, including those driven by germline APC mutation in familial adenomatous polyposis, produces dysplastic glandular proliferation that can progress from low-grade through high-grade dysplasia to invasive adenocarcinoma. As the lesion enlarges it may obstruct the biliary or pancreatic outflow, causing jaundice or pancreatitis, and its friable surface can bleed. Because dysplasia and early carcinoma can coexist within a single lesion, complete histological assessment of the excised specimen is essential.
additionalDifferentials: Ampullary adenomyoma or benign papillary stenosis
Duodenal adenoma extending to the papilla
additionalInvestigations: Side-viewing duodenoscopy with biopsy of the papilla
Endoscopic ultrasound to assess intraductal extension and local invasion
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to delineate the biliary and pancreatic ducts
Liver function tests to detect biliary obstruction
Genetic assessment and duodenal surveillance where familial adenomatous polyposis is suspected
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice or cholangitis indicating significant biliary obstruction
High-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma on histology
Intraductal extension or evidence of local invasion on endoscopic ultrasound
Recurrent pancreatitis attributable to the ampullary lesion
reference.prognosis: Completely excised benign adenomas have a good prognosis but require ongoing surveillance because of the risk of recurrence and metachronous lesions; prognosis worsens markedly once invasive carcinoma has developed.
pitfalls: Relying on superficial biopsies that miss a focus of invasive carcinoma
Attempting endoscopic resection when there is intraductal extension or frank invasion
Failing to consider familial adenomatous polyposis and arrange appropriate surveillance
Neglecting follow-up endoscopy, allowing recurrence to go undetected
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
management: Offer endoscopic papillectomy as first-line definitive treatment for adenomas without intraductal extension or invasion
Reserve pancreaticoduodenectomy for lesions with high-grade dysplasia, intraductal growth or invasive carcinoma on complete histology
Place a prophylactic pancreatic duct stent at papillectomy to reduce the risk of post-procedure pancreatitis
Relieve biliary obstruction with endoscopic stenting where jaundice or cholangitis complicates the lesion
Undertake scheduled surveillance duodenoscopy to detect local recurrence and metachronous duodenal adenomas
Arrange genetic counselling, family screening and lifelong duodenal surveillance where familial adenomatous polyposis is identified
Manage within a hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team to guide resection strategy and histological review
